Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
I've read it. This briefing is close to the position I reached across the last five replies, which makes it the one I most need to check against the sources rather than against my own summaries. Most of it holds. Where it goes wrong, it repeats claims the later sources themselves stated too strongly: the decline in the gain, the share attributed to meetings, and the "convergence" of estimates. Its bottom line, the part a working group will quote, carries two of those.

## What it says

The briefing synthesises the five sources without adding data.

**How the sources fit together:**

- Source 1's headline figures were inflated.
- Source 2 introduced the split between discretionary and coverage-bound work.
- Source 3's corrections stand, but its claims of "entirely an artifact", novelty, and no meetings effect don't.
- Source 4's subgroups converge on 8–10%, but its "no decay" claim was wrong.
- Source 5 meets the strictest standards: the gain declined to 8.5% but persists, and meetings account for 47%.

**Table 1** orders the per-hour estimates by strength of design and concludes that they stabilise at 8–10%.

**Conclusions:**

- Per hour: yes, a moderate gain of 8–10% in discretionary work.
- Per worker: no; output is about 2–4% lower, with intervals that include zero.
- Coverage-bound work: no, on any measure that matters to the people served.
- About half the gain comes from fewer meetings.
- Sickness and resignations fall in every source.

**Open questions:** whether the hours cut is necessary for the gain, what happens beyond two years, the unexplained third of the gain, manufacturing, and the private sector.

I checked the figures it cites against the sources, and they are transcribed correctly.

## What holds

These points are well supported, and the briefing states them at the right strength:

- The coverage-bound finding, called the most consistent in the body.
- The per-worker conclusion, that output is roughly maintained but not increased.
- Rejecting both slogans: that a shorter week makes people more productive, and that the gains are a mirage.
- Refusing to put a figure on how far the sickness and turnover gains offset lost output.
- Making the reorganisation question the main open item.

## Where it states more than the sources support

**1. The decline is reported as fact, using a comparison of two different measures.**

"Declined from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares nine-month timesheet hours with 24-month system-log hours. The like-for-like comparison is +12.5% to +9.8%, and its intervals (6.9 to 18.4 and 4.6 to 15.2) overlap almost entirely.

During the follow-up, two control offices cut their own meetings and improved. That narrows the treated-minus-control gap without any fading in treated offices, and could account for a meaningful part of the 2.7-point difference.

Section 4 nonetheless says, "the per-hour gain declined." The accurate statement is that the point estimate fell, the fall is not distinguishable from noise, and it is partly confounded by changes in the control offices.

**2. Calling Source 4's "no decay" claim "wrong" makes the same mistake in reverse.**

Source 5 showed that the meta-analysis's evidence for "no decay" consisted of four uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours. That makes the claim unsupported, not false. Calling it wrong and then asserting a decline closes the question in the other direction. Whether the gain is durable is still open, though it is now known to persist to at least 24 months.

**3. The meetings share is stated more firmly than Source 5's own limitations allow.**

Source 5 says it "attributed" 47% to meetings, and the briefing turns this into "about half the per-hour gain *comes from* removing recurring meetings", repeated in the bottom line. But:

- The share depends on there being no unmeasured confounding, which Source 5 itself flags.
- It rests on 7 versus 7 offices, the same offices that generated the hypothesis.
- Its interval runs from 28% to 66%.

A fair statement is that the registered mediation analysis identifies fewer meetings as the largest measured pathway, with an estimated share of between about a quarter and two-thirds.

**4. The "convergence" on 8–10% counts the same studies several times.**

The controlled, actual-hours, record-based and controlled-discretionary subgroups in Source 4 overlap heavily, and Varden is in every one of them. Listing five agreeing figures overstates how much independent evidence there is.

The 8–10% range is still a reasonable reading. It rests mainly on Varden plus a small number of controlled studies, and the briefing should say so.

**5. Table 1 isn't ordered by strength of design, and it mixes types of work.**

- The meta-analysis estimate for all studies sits below two uncontrolled subsets.
- The counter-work figure (+6.7%) sits at the bottom, presented as the strongest evidence. It is coverage-bound work, which the conclusion is not about, and placing it last makes the "estimates fall as designs strengthen" pattern look cleaner than it is.
- The like-for-like 24-month timesheet figure (+9.8%) is missing.

Separate tables for discretionary and coverage-bound work would fix the mixing. Within the discretionary table, rows can then be ranked by design.

## Points the sources raised that the briefing drops

**Per-hour gains in coverage-bound work are probably not productivity gains.** With fewer staff and unchanged opening hours, queues lengthen and occupancy rises, so contacts per hour go up while the public waits longer. Calling them "real but small" invites the wrong reading.

**The per-worker interval needs its lower end.** The interval for output per worker extends to about −8% (Varden −3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2). "Intervals include zero" is true, but a policy reader should also see how large a loss the data allow.

**The sick-day figures carry two unresolved issues:**

- The 36% comes from Halden, which is uncontrolled and was not seasonally matched.
- In four-day schedules, part of any fall may simply reflect fewer days on which sickness can be recorded, and no source addressed that.

The direction of the effect is probably real. "27 to 36%" gives its size more precision than the evidence supports.

**Continuation should be counted from enrolment.** Source 1's 92% continuation is restated without Source 3's correction. Counted from enrolment, it is 80%, and the organisations that withdrew were concentrated among those that struggled.

**The open questions are missing four items:**

- **Cost per unit of output.** Full pay, roughly 3% lower output per worker, and claimed overtime mean cost per case probably rose. No source reports it, and it is the figure a policy group most needs.
- **External validity.** Even the randomised evidence comes from an employer willing to run the trial.
- **Client-deadline work.** Source 5's reverting marketing agency suggests a third category of work: no requirement to be present, but no control over timing.
- **Contamination of the control offices** in the 24-month estimates.

## A bottom line the evidence supports

> *In discretionary work, mostly public administration, a 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raised output per actual hour by roughly 8–10% in the best-measured evidence, persisting to at least two years, while output per worker ended slightly lower (about −3%, compatible with anything from no loss to about 8%). Fewer recurring meetings are the largest measured pathway. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added, at higher cost per unit served. Whether the gain is durable beyond two years, how much is due to the hours cut itself rather than to reorganising work, and what happens to cost per unit of output, remain open.*

I can produce a revised version of the briefing with these changes made in place and marked, so the working group can see exactly what changed and why.
